description_full: Hormel Foods Corporation develops, processes, and distributes various meat, nut, and other food products to foodservice, convenience stores, and commercial customers in the United States and internationally. It operates through three segments: Retail, Foodservice, and International. The company provides perishable products, including fresh meats, frozen items, refrigerated meal solutions, bacon, sausages, hams, guacamole, and other items that require refrigeration, as well as shelf-stable products, such as canned luncheon meats, nut butters, snack nuts, chili, shelf-stable microwaveable meals, hash, stews, tortillas, salsas, tortilla chips, and other items that do not require refrigeration. It sells its products under the HORMEL, ALWAYS TENDER, APPLEGATE, AUSTIN BLUES, BACON 1, BLACK LABEL, BREAD READY, BURKE, CAFÉ H, CERATTI, CHI-CHI'S, COLUMBUS, COMPLEATS, CORN NUTS, CURE 81, DAN'S PRIZE, DI LUSSO, DINTY MOORE, DON MIGUEL, DOÑA MARIA, EMBASA, FAST N EASY, FIRE BRAISED, FONTANINI, HERDEZ, HORMEL GATHERINGS, HOUSE OF TSANG, JENNIE-O, JUSTIN'S, LA VICTORIA, LAYOUT, LLOYD'S, MARY KITCHEN, MR. PEANUT, NATURAL CHOICE, NUT-RITION, OLD SMOKEHOUSE, OVEN READY, PILLOW PACK, PLANTERS, ROSA GRANDE, SADLER'S SMOKEHOUSE, SKIPPY, SPAM, SQUARE TABLE, SPECIAL RECIPE, VALLEY FRESH, and WHOLLY brands through sales personnel, independent brokers, and distributors. The company was formerly known as Geo. A. Hormel & Company and changed its name to Hormel Foods Corporation in January 1995. Hormel Foods Corporation was founded in 1891 and is headquartered in Austin, Minnesota.

financial_summary: Hormel Foods Corporation is a large-cap consumer defensive business with a $12.2B market cap on $12.1B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -1% over the past three years and +3% annually across the full decade — essentially flat, and a business treading water is rarely a path to compounding.

Returns on capital run at 8% against a 6% cost of capital, which means the business barely earns its keep economically, and 17% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $534M in free cash flow — roughly 4 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.77× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 2.2× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 9.2×.

Management returns a meaningful 5.2% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 4.4% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 5.1% (vs the 8% bar).

growth: Revenue has compounded at -1.0% over 3 years, 4.7% over 5 years and 2.7% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
At current returns, reinvesting 43% of profits supports about 3.6% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded -6.8% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.2x, 2.6% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 9, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 7.4% on average.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.5%), and institutions hold 92%.
Insider trading is two-way: 1 purchase and 1 sale over the past year, net $294K sold.
It returns 5.2% a year to shareholders (5.3% in dividends).
It pays out 188% of earnings, more than it earns, so the dividend is at risk.
